source.title: Theoretical Insights into Overparameterized Models in Multi-Task and Replay-Based Continual Learning
source.authors: Mohammadamin Banayeeanzade; Mahdi Soltanolkotabi; Mohammad Rostami

record.tranche_reason: The study measures model-size error curves and refines the account of their peaks, reporting that task dissimilarity can contribute to a peak in addition to label noise. It tests these behaviors in multi-task and replay-based continual-learning settings.
record.gate_note: The paper cites epoch-wise double descent but fixes its own experiments at 100 epochs rather than varying training time. It discusses sample-size effects in its theory, but does not report a direct experiment establishing that adding samples raises test error near the interpolation threshold. Figure-only curves are recorded as such; cited findings from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures test error against model size in a new setting: linear and deep multi-task and replay-based continual learners. It reports that a peak at the interpolation threshold followed by a second descent appears. It also gives a theorem and experiments on what drives the peak (label noise and task dissimilarity). Its own width sweeps bear directly on V1, V4 and V6, so it tests rather than uses the finding. T3 fits better than T5: the main contribution is extending the curve to MTL/CL, and the task-dissimilarity point refines V6 rather than arguing a version is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress two further points. First, in MTL the error peak stems from task dissimilarity as well as label noise, so it appears even without noise. Second, larger models reduce forgetting but benefit less from replay memory, so model size and buffer size should be balanced. They frame the deep-network results as qualitative support for the linear theory, not as formal claims.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies multi-task and replay-based continual learning, with exact results for Gaussian-feature linear models and width sweeps of deep models on practical datasets. Its experimental setup is not the original single-task deep double-descent study.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported peak behavior or its strength and location varies with label noise, task similarity, classifier head sharing, dataset and backbone, and replay-buffer size. The paper also reports a depth-related effect on peak height.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing replay-buffer size shifts the CL test-error peak to the right and reduces its intensity. Larger models reduce forgetting and reduce the benefit of memory (Figure 6, Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In replay-based continual learning, buffer size controls the location and height of the model-wise error peak, and model size and memory size trade off.

fits_no_version.finding: MLP depth affects the height of the test-error peak in multi-head MTL (Figure 17).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The double-descent peak height depends on network depth at fixed width sweep.

record.problems: The empirical conclusions are described as qualitative rather than formal claims about deep-model performance. Curves are largely figure-based; exact curve values and uncertainty estimates are not stated in the supplied text. Experiments were repeated at least 3 times, with average results reported.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported result bearing on the tested versions was left out. Epoch-wise double descent is cited but not tested, and the discussion of sample-size effects does not report a direct more-data-causes-higher-error result.

untested.parts: All. Epochs are fixed at 100, and the authors say they did this deliberately to avoid epoch-wise effects.
No deep-network sweep of training-set size at fixed model size. Only the linear replay results speak to it indirectly.
The MTL theorem covers only the overparameterized regime (p ≥ n̄+2), so the classical U-shape side is not derived for MTL.
All. There is no single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across size, epochs and samples. The threshold is located at p = n̄ (parameters equal samples) only.
Multiple or triple descent, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.

missing.what: Single-task deep-learner test-loss curves at σ = 0, 0.1 and 0.2. The authors say the STL peak is negligible in some configurations, which bears on V1 and V6.
Linear single-task learner shows no error peak at σ = 0 and a peak growing with σ (simulated against theory).
Linear replay learner: smaller memory can beat the full-MTL learner at the MTL interpolation threshold. This is a more-data-hurts pattern.
CL label-noise sweep (m = 50, σ = 0, 0.1, 0.2): error peak intensified with stronger noise.
Depth sweep (0-3 hidden layers) changes peak height.

record.verdict_notes: All deep-network evidence is figure-only, averaged over at least 3 runs; no peak heights are given numerically. The linear theory is exact but holds only for p ≥ n̄+2; the underparameterized MTL side comes from simulation and the single-task formula. The V3 and STL-negligible-peak verdicts rest on text, not rows. The original sources (1912.02292, 1812.11118) are cited but are not this study.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests model-size curves in multi-task and replay-based continual-learning settings, not the full range of deep-network settings in the claim.
Training time or epochs are not swept; the experiments train for 100 epochs.
No direct result reports that increasing the number of training samples raises test error near an interpolation threshold.
The results concern the paper's linear multi-task model and specified deep multi-task and continual-learning experiments; they do not establish the claim across all model classes.
The paper does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The paper tests how label noise and task dissimilarity relate to the peak. It does not test multiple or triple descent, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The paper does not recalculate complexity using an effective parameter count or test whether that turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shape.
